text.p: Australia's current account deficit for December was A$1.408 billion, compared with a A$1.893 billion shortfall in November, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported. Market forecasts had centred on a deficit of A$1.78 billion, and ranged from A$1.4 to A$2.0 billion.
A selection of immediate reactions to the data follow:
DAVID DE GARIS, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"The number being right at the bottom of market expectations is a good monthly result for the Aussie dollar. Sentiment is very, very weak but of course it is so much influenced by the volatility in these monthly export numbers. So reading a new trend in the 1.4 (A$ billion deficit) would be extremely dangerous. In fact, the net income deficit continues at 1.6 (A$ billion). It certainly highlights that the underlying deficit is higher than that 1.4 (A$ billion) on an ongoing basis, but it is a good monthly result."
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA RESEARCH:

"I think the real reason I'd like to get the champagne corks out for is the fact that it was the last monthly current account release. It's certainly a release whose passing won't be mourned by many market economists. It's a good result, but these monthly numbers are reasonably volatile and we can't read too much into that eight percent rise in exports because we had to see a good export performance sometime. But what I think is pretty good about these numbers is that now we have got the full year's current account in, we've only got a deficit of about A$19.2 billion for 1996 which is much, much better than the A$26 billion that we had in 1995."
PETER MUNCKTON, SENIOR ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"Clearly some of the pessimism about the current account in some quarters recently has been overstated. Overall, this is broadly in the type of A$1.2 billion and A$1.3 billion range that it has been in for some time and it is likely to be in that range at least for the next few months. As we go through 1997 though and into 1998 the current account is likely to pick up somewhat."
BRUCE FREELAND, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"Obviously somewhat better than expected, just seeing it come in at 1.4 (A$ billion) after those couple of higher numbers. I think we are still certainly very much on track for about a A$20 billion figure for the year (1996/97 to June 30), and in some ways it's not a bad sort of figure to see out the monthly current account deficit's passing. The particularly good news obviously is that big jump in exports across the board."
JOHN PETERS, MARKET ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"We weren't expecting such a rise in exports, but it's not going to alter our view at all. It keeps us on track for a current account deficit of A$20 billion for 1996/97, which is in line with the government's forecast."
